title: Harris-Benedict BMR Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate your basal metabolic rate using the Harris-Benedict formula. Free online BMR calculator to estimate daily calories burned at rest.
intro: Your basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the number of calories your body burns over 24 hours at complete rest just to keep you alive: heart pumping, lungs breathing, brain firing, kidneys filtering, cells dividing. For most US adults, BMR accounts for roughly 60 to 70 percent of total daily calorie burn, which is why nailing this number is the first step in any sensible weight loss, weight gain, or body recomposition plan. This calculator runs the Harris-Benedict equation, originally published by Harris and Benedict at the Carnegie Institution in 1919 and revised by Roza and Shizgal in 1984 to better fit modern body sizes. The revised Harris-Benedict equation is still used in clinical practice and on most fitness apps, but research suggests the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (published in 1990) tends to be slightly more accurate for the average US adult; the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics endorses Mifflin-St Jeor as the current best practice for non-obese adults. For athletes with known body fat percentage, the Katch-McArdle formula based on lean body mass is more precise. Typical BMR values run 1,600 to 2,000 calories per day for US men and 1,300 to 1,700 calories per day for US women, with substantial individual variation driven by height, lean mass, and age. Enter your stats in pounds and inches; we convert internally and show the result in plain calories.
keyTakeaway: The Harris-Benedict formula estimates how many calories your body burns at rest based on age, weight, height, and sex. Multiply your BMR by an activity factor to get TDEE, then add or subtract calories to lose or gain weight.
useCases: Cutting: calculate a 300 to 500 calorie daily deficit below TDEE to lose roughly 0.5 to 1 lb of fat per week without nuking metabolism
Bulking: calculate a 250 to 500 calorie surplus above TDEE to add lean mass while minimizing fat gain, typical lean bulk pace 0.5 to 1 lb per month
Registered dietitian intake assessment: cross-check a client's reported food log against estimated needs to flag underreporting or chronic underfeeding

Calibrating a fitness tracker: Apple Watch, Fitbit, Garmin, and WHOOP all run their own BMR estimate; compare against Harris-Benedict and Mifflin-St Jeor to see if your device is over or underestimating
Pre-bariatric or medical weight loss intake planning: clinicians use BMR as the floor under which medical supervision becomes necessary
Sports nutrition for high school and collegiate athletes: BMR plus activity multiplier gives a starting point for fueling two-a-day training blocks
explanation:
## What BMR Actually Measures

Basal metabolic rate is the energy your body spends doing nothing. It is measured in a lab after 12 hours of fasting, eight hours of sleep, and 30 minutes of supine rest in a thermoneutral room, typically using indirect calorimetry to capture oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production. Outside the lab, we estimate it with prediction equations like Harris-Benedict. BMR powers involuntary work: pumping blood (the heart alone burns about 440 calories a day), maintaining body temperature, running the brain (roughly 20 percent of BMR in a healthy adult), kidney filtration, liver detoxification, and constant cellular turnover. It does not include the thermic effect of food (TEF, about 10 percent of daily calories) or any physical activity. RMR (resting metabolic rate) is a closely related cousin: it is measured under less strict conditions (no overnight fast or pre-test rest period required) and runs about 10 percent higher than true BMR. In practice, most calculators and fitness apps use the terms interchangeably even though they are not identical.

## The Harris-Benedict Revised (1984) Formulas

The revised Harris-Benedict equation, the one we run here, uses metric units internally:

**Men:** BMR = 88.362 + (13.397 x weight in kg) + (4.799 x height in cm) - (5.677 x age in years)

**Women:** BMR = 447.593 + (9.247 x weight in kg) + (3.098 x height in cm) - (4.330 x age in years)

To convert from US units: divide pounds by 2.205 to get kilograms, multiply inches by 2.54 to get centimeters. For a 35-year-old man weighing 180 lb at 6'0" (180 lb / 2.205 = 81.6 kg, 72 in x 2.54 = 182.9 cm): BMR = 88.362 + (13.397 x 81.6) + (4.799 x 182.9) - (5.677 x 35) = 88.362 + 1,093.2 + 877.7 - 198.7 = approximately 1,861 calories per day. That is what his body would burn lying perfectly still for 24 hours.

## Mifflin-St Jeor (1990): The More Accurate Modern Standard

Mifflin et al. published an updated equation in 1990 that better matches contemporary US adults; the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (AND) recommends it as the current best practice for non-obese individuals:

**Men:** BMR = (10 x weight in kg) + (6.25 x height in cm) - (5 x age in years) + 5

**Women:** BMR = (10 x weight in kg) + (6.25 x height in cm) - (5 x age in years) - 161

For that same 180 lb, 6'0", 35-year-old man: BMR = (10 x 81.6) + (6.25 x 182.9) - (5 x 35) + 5 = 816 + 1,143 - 175 + 5 = approximately 1,789 calories. About 70 calories lower than Harris-Benedict, which is the typical gap; Harris-Benedict tends to slightly overestimate compared with Mifflin-St Jeor on most modern populations.

## Katch-McArdle: For Athletes With Body Fat Data

If you know your body fat percentage (DEXA scan, BodPod, or a high-quality bioimpedance device), Katch-McArdle uses lean body mass and is more accurate for muscular people who are systematically underestimated by weight-based formulas:

BMR = 370 + (21.6 x lean body mass in kg), where lean body mass = total weight x (1 - body fat percent / 100)

## From BMR to TDEE: The Activity Multipliers

BMR is calories at rest; total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) adds movement on top. Multiply BMR by one of these activity factors:

- **Sedentary (1.2):** desk job, little to no exercise, mostly seated day
- **Lightly active (1.375):** light exercise or sports 1-3 days per week, or a job with regular walking
- **Moderately active (1.55):** moderate exercise 3-5 days per week, common for recreational gym-goers
- **Very active (1.725):** hard exercise 6-7 days per week, common for serious lifters and endurance athletes
- **Extra active (1.9):** very hard exercise plus a physically demanding job or two-a-day training

For the 1,861-calorie BMR man above doing moderate exercise four days a week, TDEE is approximately 1,861 x 1.55 = 2,884 calories. To lose 1 lb per week (3,500 calorie deficit, divided by 7 days = 500 calories per day), he would eat 2,384 calories per day.

## Limitations and When These Equations Fail

Prediction equations assume an average body composition. They systematically underestimate BMR in very lean and muscular people (a 200 lb bodybuilder at 8 percent body fat has far more lean mass than the equation assumes) and overestimate in people with low lean mass relative to total weight, including some obese individuals. They also miss meaningful BMR shifts from thyroid disorders (hypothyroidism lowers BMR roughly 10 to 20 percent, hyperthyroidism raises it), prolonged severe dieting (adaptive thermogenesis can drop measured RMR 5 to 15 percent below predicted after a long cut), pregnancy and lactation (which raise needs substantially), and certain medications including beta blockers and stimulants. If your weight is not responding to a calculated calorie target after two to three weeks of consistent tracking, the equation is probably off for you; adjust intake by 100 to 200 calories and reassess rather than assuming the formula is gospel.

faq.q: Harris-Benedict vs Mifflin-St Jeor: which formula is better?
faq.a: Mifflin-St Jeor (1990) is generally considered more accurate for modern US adults and is the formula endorsed by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics for non-obese individuals. A 2005 systematic review found Mifflin-St Jeor predicted measured RMR within 10 percent in about 82 percent of non-obese adults, versus around 69 percent for the original Harris-Benedict. The 1984 revised Harris-Benedict closed much of that gap but Mifflin-St Jeor still edges it out on average. Both formulas land within roughly 50 to 100 calories of each other for most adults, so for practical diet planning the difference is small. Use Mifflin-St Jeor if you have to pick one; use Harris-Benedict if a clinician or program specifically asks for it.

faq.q: Is the BMR calculator accurate for muscular or very lean people?
faq.a: No, both Harris-Benedict and Mifflin-St Jeor underestimate BMR for muscular individuals because they only use total body weight and do not distinguish lean mass from fat mass. A 200 lb male athlete at 10 percent body fat has 180 lb of lean mass; a 200 lb sedentary male at 30 percent body fat has 140 lb of lean mass. Their BMRs can differ by 200 calories or more even though the equation gives the same answer. If you are clearly more muscular than average, use the Katch-McArdle formula, which uses lean body mass directly; you will need a body fat percentage from DEXA, BodPod, or a high-quality bioimpedance scan. As a quick correction, athletes often run 5 to 10 percent above the Mifflin-St Jeor estimate.

faq.q: What is the BMR for a 180 lb man who is 6'0" tall?
faq.a: Using the Harris-Benedict revised formula for a 35-year-old 180 lb (81.6 kg) 6'0" (182.9 cm) man: BMR is approximately 1,861 calories per day. Using Mifflin-St Jeor, it is approximately 1,789 calories per day. The gap of about 70 calories is normal between the two equations. Age affects this significantly: at age 25 the same man would have a BMR around 1,917 (Harris-Benedict) or 1,839 (Mifflin-St Jeor); at age 55 it drops to roughly 1,748 or 1,689. To get total daily calorie needs, multiply by an activity factor between 1.2 (sedentary) and 1.9 (extra active).

faq.q: How many calories do I need to eat to lose 1 lb per week?
faq.a: One pound of body fat stores about 3,500 calories of energy, so a 500 calorie daily deficit (500 x 7 = 3,500) theoretically yields 1 lb of fat loss per week. Start by calculating your TDEE (BMR multiplied by your activity factor), then subtract 500 calories. For a typical 30-year-old US woman, 150 lb, 5'5", lightly active: BMR is about 1,420, TDEE is about 1,953, target intake for 1 lb per week loss is about 1,450 calories per day. In practice, expect 0.5 to 1.5 lb per week actual loss; the 3,500 calorie rule is a useful approximation but adaptive thermogenesis, water shifts, and tracking error all create noise. Do not drop below your BMR without medical supervision, and aim for no more than 1 percent of body weight lost per week to preserve muscle.

faq.q: What is the difference between RMR and BMR?
faq.a: BMR (basal metabolic rate) is measured after a 12-hour fast, full overnight sleep, and 30 minutes of supine rest in a thermoneutral lab, capturing the absolute minimum energy needed to stay alive. RMR (resting metabolic rate) is measured under less strict conditions: no overnight fast or pre-test rest required, just sit quietly for a few minutes before testing. RMR runs about 10 percent higher than true BMR because digestion (TEF) and minor activity are still happening. Outside the lab, most calculators and apps use RMR and BMR interchangeably, which is fine for diet planning since the difference is smaller than the equation's prediction error. If a clinical report distinguishes the two, take BMR as the cleaner baseline.

faq.q: Do the activity multipliers overestimate my real calorie burn?
faq.a: Often, yes. The standard multipliers (1.2 to 1.9) were developed in the late 20th century and many people, especially those tracking moderate gym attendance, overstate their activity. A common pattern: someone with a desk job who works out 4 days a week picks the 1.55 moderately active multiplier, but their non-exercise activity (NEAT) is actually low because they sit for 9 hours. A more conservative starting estimate is to use one tier lower than feels right (e.g., 1.375 instead of 1.55) and adjust based on real-world weight change over 2 to 3 weeks. Fitness trackers can help but their calorie burn estimates have their own 10 to 30 percent error margins, especially during strength training.

faq.q: Should I ever eat below my BMR to lose weight faster?
faq.a: Generally not, and not without medical supervision. Eating below BMR for extended periods (weeks to months) is associated with adaptive thermogenesis (your body lowers RMR 5 to 15 percent below predicted to defend against perceived starvation), muscle loss, fatigue, hormonal disruption (lower thyroid output, lower testosterone or estrogen, menstrual irregularity), and increased risk of regaining weight after the diet ends. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics recommends a moderate deficit of 500 to 750 calories below TDEE for most adults wanting to lose weight, which usually keeps intake above BMR. Very low calorie diets (VLCDs) below 800 calories total are clinically appropriate in specific circumstances like pre-bariatric surgery prep, but only under physician oversight.

faq.q: Does BMR change with age, and can I do anything about it?
faq.a: BMR drops roughly 1 to 2 percent per decade after age 20, mostly because of gradual loss of lean muscle mass (sarcopenia) and to a lesser extent reduced organ activity. A 60-year-old will typically have a BMR 100 to 200 calories lower than they did at 25 at the same body weight. The good news: this is largely preventable. Resistance training 2 to 3 times per week preserves and rebuilds muscle, blunting most of the drop. Adequate protein intake (0.7 to 1 g per lb of body weight for active adults) supports muscle maintenance. Cardio supports cardiovascular health but does not preserve BMR the way strength training does. Older adults who lift weights regularly often have BMRs comparable to sedentary 30-year-olds at the same body weight.

faq.q: How often should I recalculate my BMR?
faq.a: Recalculate any time your weight changes by more than 5 to 10 lb, since weight is the largest variable in the equation. Also recalculate on each birthday milestone (every 5 years) to account for age effects. If you are actively dieting or bulking, recalculate every 4 to 6 weeks as your weight changes. The formula itself does not need updating: Harris-Benedict revised (1984) and Mifflin-St Jeor (1990) have not been superseded by any new standard. What does change is your individual response, so treat the calculated number as a starting estimate and adjust based on 2 to 3 weeks of consistent tracking and real weight trend.
